utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Very well. Good afternoon. We are all here, the same people as the morning, this afternoon at the Status Conference. We are going to deal at least with the following items, if the agenda and the time allow us, but I should like really not to work beyond 5.30. Perhaps we shall not be able to cover all the matters by that time, and therefore perhaps we shall have to continue tomorrow, perhaps some other day. However, tomorrow we already have some other business at 4.00 so that we shall have to do it at a later stage. First, we shall consider the Prosecutor's motion regarding the modification of the list of witnesses of the Prosecution. This is the motion of the 21st of August. Secondly, the Prosecution's motion for protective measures of the 21st and 28th of August. Thirdly, the motion of Zigic's Defence of the 20th of August, 2000 regarding the admission of Exhibit D21/1. Fifth, the consolidation of the indictment, and we shall see at least to do it today. Perhaps this is not yet finished. Then the sixth point is the request, that is, complementing the expert testimony. Then the affidavits, the matter of affidavits which the Prosecution mentioned today, and it has documents to submit. Then we have the calendar, the documents and the matter of language which the Defence also wanted to raise. So perhaps we should begin from the beginning, and it is practically even logical to begin with the admission of exhibits. We've already made some progress in the discussions. So the first point is the Prosecution's motion regarding the modification of the list of witnesses of the 21st of August. The Prosecutor wishes to modify the witness list of the 28th of April, under Article 73 bis (D). The new list features 11 new witness names. Eighteen witnesses who are on the list of the 28th of April, they are being suppressed. The Prosecutor wishes to present affidavits for these 18 witnesses who have been stricken off the list and not to call these witnesses unless their affidavits are challenged. The Chamber received the answer of Mr. Kos' Defence, and they say that this motion had arrived too late and it lacks grounds. However, I should like to hear from the Prosecutor, from the Defence as well. But from the Prosecution in the first place, I shall like some precision. This modification comes following suit of the judicial notice, taking note of certain facts and saying that it was not allowed to submit a new list of witnesses, bearing in mind adjudicated facts. We understood that the list would be cut down. A small question, therefore, to the Prosecution: Do you believe that the affidavits will be challenged and that one will have to call 18 witnesses in addition to those 11 witnesses, or if they are not challenged, then there will be no changes? Another question, to the Defence this time, is as follows: Do the Defence counsel of other accused have any objections to the Prosecutor's motion? As I have said, we have received only the objections from the counsel of Mr. Kos. Therefore, I should like to hear whether this is a general objection, and I should like to see how the communication works, really. Was that the objection on behalf of all the counsel of the Defence? Is that how we should understand it? Yes? Very well. Yes, I understand. You may answer, of course, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, we have discussed this response and our position with my colleagues, and the position is this: I will speak in support of the reply, and if my colleagues have anything to add -- there will be no repetition to what I have said. They may, however, wish briefly to address issues that we did not touch upon, but there will be no repetition if they speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you for this clarification, Mr. O'Sullivan. Very well. Now I shall give the floor to Mr. Keegan who will now explain to us, very briefly because we do have the written document, but nevertheless, we should like to ask you to make these clarifications. You have the floor, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Given the lengthy agenda we have, of course, I would not like to repeat what was stated in our motion. I would say that as a general matter, the request to revise flows, as we indicate, from the developments of the case as it has gone, in particular with respect to the acceptance of the adjudicated facts, and also some additional evidence which has developed, for example, the forensic evidence, that is, based on the forensic reports, the identification of remains from graves in Kevljani, for example, which relate to victims from Omarska. And my focus -- my attention, rather, to the Defence general objection or the response filed and perhaps answer some of the questions in that manner. And as we see it, the Defence objection really falls into two categories: One, they indicate that this request is in violation of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence; and that second, as a matter of principle, it prejudices the accused in a fashion that would render it a violation of Article 21, or Articles 20 and 21. In the first instance, the -- our proposal, the motion, does not violate either Rules 65 ter or 73 bis. On the contrary, both of those rules envision, in fact, this very request. 65 ter, Rule 65 ter, of course, must be read in conjunction with Rule 66(A)(ii), which is the disclosure rule; and Rule 66(A)(ii) says specifically that statements of additional Prosecution witnesses shall be made available when the decision is made to call those witnesses. That decision, as it flows from the plain meaning and the language of that rule, would flow after the original disclosure and after the original time limit for objections to the indictment, et cetera, have run. Secondly, Rule 73 bis (D) specifically contemplates such a motion wherein it states that the Prosecutor may, if she believes it to be in the interests of justice, revise the witness list after the commencement of the trial. So this request is, in the first instance, entirely in accord with the rules and procedure and evidence at this Tribunal. As to the second issue, the Defence raises a number of issues. They cite, for example, the issue of equality of arms, and they focus in particular on the right from Article 21 of the Defence, the right of the accused to adequate time for case preparation and Defence. Yes, case preparation and equal treatment of the accused. It is the Prosecution's position that the citations to Article 20 are, in fact, the correct citations. Article 20 indicates that the Trial Chamber shall ensure that the trial is conducted in a fair and expeditious fashion and in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, with due regard for the protection -- full respect of the rights of the accused and due regard for the protection of victims and witnesses. Plainly speaking, Article 20 indicates that both sides have the right to a fair and expeditious trial that is conducted in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Well, this request is entirely in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and is entirely in accordance with the way proceedings may develop as envisioned in the rules. The Defence cites, too, the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision and cites with respect to the issue of the equality of arms. They cite to paragraph 47 and 48 -- excuse me, paragraphs 48 and 49 -- I'm sorry, 48 and 47. They did not, of course, go to paragraph 49 and to paragraph 52 which we would submit are also applicable here. No one, of course, argues with the position that the Defence here, the accused in any case, must not be placed in a position which is of substantial disadvantage to the Prosecution, but as recognised by the Appeals Chamber, that is, of course, with respect to matters and issues which are under the supervision and within the control of a Trial Chamber. The decision also indicates, of course, that this issue of equality of arms and this issue of fairness with respect to position relates to both parties. Finally, in paragraph 52, the Appeals Chamber recognised that the principle of equality of arms as applied to the International Tribunal must be given a rather more liberal interpretation than that when being applied to States, in particular because of the different position of the Trial Chambers with respect to their powers and authorities vis-à-vis States and their ability to influence witnesses' evidence, the production of evidence, et cetera. Whereas we are entirely dependent on cooperation, national courts obviously are not. We raise these issues because we believe that this Trial Chamber is fully aware of the difficulties that both parties face with respect to dealing with witnesses and the production of witnesses for trials, the logistical issues, the current affairs issues, if you will, with respect to relocation, the situation within the territories in the former Yugoslavia, et cetera, all of which impact on witnesses' availability or even willingness to testify. And those factors fluctuate and change depending on the circumstances of the individual witnesses, sometimes the development of a particular case, and sometimes just through the persistence of the parties and their ability to themselves influence events and perhaps persuade witnesses to actually appear. The Prosecution submits that the general issue of Article 20 is, of course, always applicable, and that is the issue of a fair trial for both parties. With respect, we think the issue of equality of arms in a technical sense is in opposite here. There has been no denial of procedural rights to either party, and there has been no denial of any substantive rights. The question here then really falls to the underlying question which is present with any request from either party for deviation in process in the trial proceedings, and that is, is there substantial prejudice to one party or the other which cannot be cured in some fashion. And we believe that is the only question that's of relevance here because that is really the last basis which the Defence raises, and that is the question of prejudice to the accused, and they focus on the issue of adequate time to prepare a defence. And while they raise the issue, they then fail entirely to point to any prejudice that would arise. And we submit the reason why there is a complete dearth of information on that point is because they can't claim any real prejudice because there are too many obvious remedies which would be applicable here, short of denying the Prosecution its right to present the best evidence which it can with respect to the indictment. There is no indication that they would even need any delay in the proceedings to prepare for these witnesses in the first instance. Secondly, if there was a need to prepare for the testimony of these witnesses, there's no indication of how long they would need. And third, even if they do need some time, there's no indication that that would necessarily be -- that time would have a prejudicial effect either on the accused or on the Prosecution, or indeed the Trial Chamber, with respect to the progress of this trial. Therefore, we believe that the motion should be granted. It's in accord with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It is in accord with the interests of justice and the fairness of the proceedings for both parties. That would be all we have at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Keegan. I think that Mr. O'Sullivan is going to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe Your Honours have received our response dated August 25th, and I would be referring to both my response and the Prosecution motion of the 21st of August. Your Honour, we oppose the calling of eight witnesses. You will note that on page 2 of the response, there are nine names or nine witnesses referred to. Witness AR was identified to us today, and we take no objection. We have no objection to Witness AR being called. Therefore, our objection is limited to the other eight witnesses who, for the record, are Witness AO, Witness AP, Witness AQ, Witness AS, Witness F, (redacted), Nihad Haskic, and (redacted). I will be referring to these witnesses collectively as the new witnesses in my oral submissions, as we have done in our written submissions. We are asking Your Honours to deny the Prosecution request for a variance in regards to these eight witnesses, the new witnesses. We ask that you preclude the Prosecution from calling them. Why these new witnesses? In our submission, allowing these witnesses to testify would amount to a violation of the rights of the accused under the Statute and Rules, including the principles of fundamental fairness, equal treatment, equality of arms, timely disclosure, and adequate time for case preparation. These new witnesses were disclosed to the Defence, their names were disclosed to the Defence for the first time in August 2000. The statements and proffers of the new witnesses are incomplete, according to the Prosecution motion, and the disclosure process began in August 2000. Your Honours, if we put this request by the Prosecution in context, and I propose to do that for you, it is patently unfair and, I submit, the prejudice is manifest. What is the context? Let's look at the history of these proceedings. Let's look at the history of the case management, case preparation and disclosure regarding Prosecution witnesses. In our response at point 1, you have paragraphs A through N, you will see, Your Honours, that in June and November, at two times, the Prosecution disclosed 186 witness statements to the Defence. None of the new witnesses are included in that list. From that point on, the case was prepared and organised and managed based on those 186 witnesses. First, I draw your attention to the filing under the old Rule 73 bis whereby the Prosecution files summaries. Hundreds of pages were prepared in anticipation of what those witnesses would say. Those summaries were disclosed; I believe a copy was provided to the Chamber. Let's look at February 14th, 2000, two weeks before this trial began. A witness list is compiled with 71 witnesses and 24 alternatives. All those individuals are from the original 186. February 23rd, 2000, less than one week before the trial begins. Under Rule 65 ter, the Prosecution files a submission listing names, pseudonyms of witnesses, areas of testimony, points on the indictment they will testify to, the counts, the paragraphs. In that document, Your Honours will see, the Prosecution took the following position: They said they would either call the 71 listed witnesses or the alternatives. April 28th, 2000, a revised witness list. By this point, the fifth accused is joined to this case. The first Prosecution witness has not yet testified. I remind you the first witness was called on May 4th. This list contains 67 witnesses, 34 alternatives. Each and every one of those individuals is part of the original 186 disclosed witnesses from 1999. No new witnesses are in that list. Now, let's contrast that with what we received just in the last several weeks from the Prosecution. I refer to Witness AO. We received that person's name for the first time on August 3rd. There is a proffer dated July 20. We receive an extract of a proffer, not a full proffer, an extract of a proffer, the 21st of August, last week. Witness AP: We've had no disclosure but for, again, an extract of a proffer on the 21st of August, 2000, last week. Witness AQ: We received an OTP statement August 18th. That statement was taken in March 1999. We see it for the first time two weeks ago. We also received an extract, not the full proffer, of this same witness August 21st, last week. Witness AS: No disclosure, nothing. Witness F: We received two statements August 3rd, 2000. One of those statements is dated 1994; the second statement is dated 1992. Never heard of this witness before; never seen those statements before. (redacted): We receive a statement August 11th, this year. The statement is dated 1996. We received another statement, August 11th of this year, dated 1998. As well, an extract of a proffer from last week. Nihad Haskic: A statement disclosed to us on August 3rd, 2000. That statement was taken in 1994. A proffer was disclosed on that same day, August 3rd, 2000; the proffer is dated 1998. We also have an extract of a proffer dated 21 August 2000. Finally, (redacted): No disclosure but for an extract dated 21 August 2000 which we received last week. My friend has suggested that under the principle of equality of arms, only matters over which the Trial Chamber has control may you decide. Well, I submit that you clearly have control over this matter. You have an obligation, in my submission, to uphold the rights of the accused to a fair trial, to timely disclosure. We do rely on the Tadic appeal decision for the principle of equality of arms and not placing the accused unfairly at a disadvantage vis-à-vis the Prosecutor. We also rely on that same Tadic decision for the proposition that, under Rule 21(4)(b), the accused is required to the right to have adequate time to prepare. Counsel is in The Hague. We are preparing for the final phase, the final six weeks of the Prosecution case. We just ended a six-week recess. This trial has been going on for six months. This matter has been before this Tribunal, including the pre-trial, for two and a half years. There can be no serious suggestion that now we have to somehow prepare for these eight witnesses at this late stage. That is completely unreasonable. There's been no timely disclosure. Your Honours, I've mentioned Rule 73 bis, the previous version, where summaries were provided. I've mentioned Rule 65 ter and that submission made by the Prosecution. Your Honours, the Prosecution knows its case, and it made a decision when it chose the witnesses it said would prove its case. Many of the statements I've referred to regarding these new witnesses date from 1994 and 1996. This Tribunal opened in 1994. Some of them date from 1992 where they were taken in Zagreb. Let's not forget that this Office of the Prosecution has tried the Tadic case. The Kovacevic case was started and not finished. The Prosecution is about to start the Keraterm case. No one can say seriously that the Prosecution does not know and has not investigated events in Prijedor municipality, in Omarska in particular. They know its witnesses, they know its case, and we say they made a decision. Now, my friend says he relies on Rule 73 bis (D), the current version. In my submission, that provides no basis for what he is attempting to do here at the eleventh hour. In my submission, Rule 73 bis (D) refers to the Pre-Trial Conference. That's the conference that's held, as you know, before the Trial Chamber. But the Pre-Trial Conference, that Rule must be read in conjunction with Rule 65 ter. Rule 65 ter is the Rule according to which, during the pre-trial phase, issues are narrowed, points of common ground are found, disputes are identified, and the witnesses are chosen by the Prosecution. Now, my friend has relied on Rule 66(A)(ii) that says that disclosure must be made as and when -- I'm paraphrasing -- as and when the Prosecution discloses. In my respectful submission, it's the reading of Rule 73 bis (D) and 65 ter which are determinative. Your Honours will know that Rule 65 ter was added to our Rules in 1998 in an attempt to expedite and streamline matters pre-trial because matters run slowly here, and Rule 65 ter was designed to accomplish that. We went all through this process over the last two years in this case with this procedure under Rule 65 ter. Now, what does 73 bis (D) say? Well, if you look at Rule 73 bis, it contemplates that at the Pre-Trial Conference, the Trial Chamber is telling the Prosecution, "You have to pare down your witnesses." Those are the witnesses that the Prosecution has chosen at the pre-trial stage under Rule 65 ter. That is why I looked at the history of these proceedings, to show you that we started with 186 witnesses that they said were their best, and they brought that down, with full disclosure, timely disclosure, in 1999. Here we are, six months into a trial, about to begin the final phase, and they're dropping new names on us, disclosing statements for the first time, all of which are years old, and that is prejudicial, that is unfair, and that is not right. That is what Your Honours are there to do in part, and that is to uphold the fair trial provisions, give meaning to the Rules of the pre-trial management which are designed to have smooth-running trials. We don't want adjournments for further investigation. We're here to finish this case based on the way it started when all of these disclosures were made, positions were taken, points were negotiated between the parties and streamlined pre-trial and Pre-Trial Conference. Your Honours, we respectfully request that you deny this motion in regard to these new witnesses. It's contrary to the Rules and Statutes to do otherwise. There is no basis to accede to the request by the Prosecution, and the Prosecution has given no sound or compelling reasons why you should do it. I won't repeat paragraphs 9 and 10 of my response, but we say that there is no basis for doing this and they have not given any sound reasons for requesting it. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. It seems that there are some additional remarks to be made by Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my additional remarks concern the part that concerns the accused Radic. I'm sure you know what I have in mind, the sexual violence crimes. We have been given a new list of the witnesses. One of them is supposed to be heard on the day after tomorrow, in two day's time. We are all here, and it is -- it should be -- we should have enough time to prepare for the witness. We didn't know his or her name, and I don't know what is the use of our presence here? What is the reason why we are here? So that one day one can say that the accused had their legal representatives. As for the fact that the Defence did not have the time to adequately prepare themselves, that seems not to be relevant. And I do not wish to be a mere decoration in this courtroom. Let me give a very brief example. In the initial indictment pursuant to which the accused were arrested, the accused Radic had only Witness A to testify against him. She did testify under her real name in the Tadic case. I see that she -- that her name has been skipped for the third time by the Prosecutor. So we have spent two years investigating the case, together with our members of the team, and you will see -- once this witness takes the stand, you will see that we have a number of documents and witnesses that we have had access to in order to investigate that witness. This means that we need some serious work to be done in respect of each and -- each and every one witness. This witness testified under her real name in the Tadic case. So the problem for me is, how am I able to examine Witness AO, who will be heard for the first time in this case, and you will see that she has not been mentioned by any of the witnesses in the present case so far. My colleague, Mr. Stojanovic and I, we have been prevented from doing our work. We simply sit here in this courtroom, and we are kept in the dark as far as the identity of the witnesses is concerned. We will be severely prejudiced if you should accept the motion of the Prosecutor. Nine years have gone by since the relevant events. Two cases were tried here before this Tribunal, hundreds of statements were collected, and let me remind you that the report concerning the camps of Omarska and Keraterm constituted the very foundation for the establishment of this Tribunal, and now we are in year 2000, in the month of August, and they need to call a new witness. This will be unfair. And let me reiterate the request of Mr. O'Sullivan: We are not here to postpone or to ask for a postponement of the trial. We are here to finish with the trial as expeditiously as possible. This is the way I understand my duty here, and therefore we have to respectfully ask you to reject the motion submitted by the Prosecutor. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Mr. Stojanovic would like to take the floor, so it seems. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much, Your Honours. I fully agree with my colleagues, Mr. O'Sullivan and Mr. Fila; however, we have a particular argument to make in respect of (redacted) (redacted).He has been proposed as the new witness, and he is the father of (redacted), who is his son and whose name also figures on the list of witnesses. In paragraph 10 in the motion of the Prosecutor, let me just quote the sentence which is contained therein that,"(redacted) would testify to if he becomes unavailable." So it is requested, it's been requested that the witness testifies on the same -- about the same events that his son has already testified about, and it is made conditional on the availability of the first witness to testify. As far as we can see, the situation is completely different now. (redacted) is supposed to testify first, and we are by no means ready to cross-examine this witness who is likely to take the stand this week or the following week, whereas (redacted) is supposed to testify later on. So as it is stated in the motion of the Prosecutor, this is the witness who would -- who is supposed to testify about the same events and same circumstances as his son who was proposed as a witness initially and whose name is still contained in the witness list. That would be our submission. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Jovan Simic, I don't know if we have an issue of protective measures here because names are being mentioned and family relations as well. I don't know if this is likely to constitute a problem. I'm sorry, Mr. Simic, but there may have been some redactions to be made because this is all in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there will need to be redactions made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we should go into private session for this purpose if names are going to be mentioned and repeated. Let us go into private session, please.
